title: Caliphate of Córdoba
capsule: The Caliphate of Córdoba was proclaimed on 16 January 929 when Abd al-Rahman III, having reunified al-Andalus after decades of civil war and rejecting both Abbasid and Fatimid authority, took the titles of caliph and Commander of the Faithful. Under Abd al-Rahman III (r. 912–961) and his son al-Hakam II (r. 961–976), Córdoba became the largest city in western Europe, its new palace-city of Medina Azahara housing a brilliant court of scholars, while the caliphate held the Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia at bay and projected influence into the Maghreb. The state unravelled after the death in 1002 of the regent al-Mansur: a Berber revolt and protracted civil war (the fitna) led to the caliphate's formal abolition in 1031, after which al-Andalus splintered into the taifa kingdoms.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core Iberian territory is well-attested through administrative and fiscal records; the extent of suzerainty over North African Berber polities fluctuated and the polygon's Maghrebi component should be treated as indicative of influence rather than administered territory.
